code.title: Built-in types: sizes, ranges, double vs decimal, overflow

followUps:
Because double stores numbers in base 2, and 0.1, 0.2 and 0.3 cannot be written exactly in base 2, just as 1/3 cannot be written exactly in base 10.

Each literal is rounded to the nearest value that fits in 64 bits. The two small errors add up, so 0.1 + 0.2 gives 0.30000000000000004, while the literal 0.3 is stored as 0.29999999999999999. They differ in the last bit, so == is false.

Two fixes: for money use decimal (base 10, 0.1m + 0.2m == 0.3m is true); for measurements compare with a tolerance, Math.Abs(a - b) < 1e-9.

There is no difference: int is the C# keyword for the .NET type System.Int32, and the compiler turns one into the other.

typeof(int) == typeof(System.Int32) is true, and int.Parse("5") and Int32.Parse("5") call the same method. The same holds for long/Int64, string/String, bool/Boolean and object/Object.

The usual style is the keyword everywhere (int count, string.IsNullOrEmpty). The Int32 name makes the size clear, which some teams like in file formats and interop code.

By default it wraps around silently: adding 1 to int.MaxValue (2,147,483,647) gives int.MinValue (-2,147,483,648), with no exception.

The extra bit is simply dropped, which is fast but can hide bugs, for example a total that suddenly turns negative.

  • Wrap the maths in checked( ... ) or a checked { } block and it throws OverflowException instead.
  • If the overflow is in a constant expression, such as int.MaxValue + 1 written directly, the compiler reports an error.
  • double never throws: it goes to Infinity. decimal always throws.

If the value can be large, use long.

code.title: Value types copy the data, reference types copy the reference

followUps:
A string is a reference type: the variable holds a reference to an object on the heap.

It feels like a value for two reasons:

  • It is immutable. No method can change the characters. s2 += "!" builds a new string and points s2 at it, so s1 never changes. Sharing one object is therefore safe.
  • == compares the characters, not the references, because string overloads the operator. "ab" == new string(new[] {'a','b'}) is true.

You can still see that it is a reference type: it can be null, and assigning it copies 8 bytes (the reference), not the text.

It lives on the heap, inside the object it belongs to.

"Value types live on the stack" is only true for local variables and parameters. A value type is stored where it is declared:

  • a local int in a method: on the stack (or in a CPU register);
  • an int field of a class: inside that object on the heap;
  • an int in an int[]: inside the array on the heap;
  • a local captured by a lambda or used in an async method: moved into a compiler-made object on the heap.

So class Order { int Qty; } puts Qty on the heap with the rest of the order.

The caller sees the change, because the method received a copy of the reference, and both references point at the same object.

void Rename(Person p) { p.Name = "Bo"; }      // caller sees "Bo"
void Swap(Person p)   { p = new Person(); }   // caller sees nothing

The second method only points its own local copy at a new object. The caller's variable still points at the old one. To let a method replace the caller's variable, pass it with ref.

With a struct the whole value is copied, so a property change inside the method is lost unless you pass it with ref.

code.title: Boxing copies a value into a heap object; unboxing needs the exact type

followUps:
No. int overrides ToString(), so the call goes straight to that method and no box is created.

Boxing happens when the value has to be treated as object or as an interface:

  • object o = n; or passing n to a parameter of type object, for example string.Format("{0}", n);
  • n.GetType(), because GetType is defined on object and cannot be overridden;
  • IComparable c = n;;
  • calling ToString() on your own struct that does not override it.

So n.ToString() is the cheap way to turn a number into text.

Because unboxing is not a conversion: it only checks that the box holds exactly the type you named and then copies the bytes out.

A box made from an int holds 4 bytes labelled Int32. (long)boxed asks for a box labelled Int64, the check fails, and you get InvalidCastException.

object boxed = 42;
long a = (long)boxed;            // throws
long b = (long)(int)boxed;       // unbox, then widen: 42
long c = Convert.ToInt64(boxed); // also 42

The same cast on a plain int variable works, because there the compiler knows the type and emits a real conversion.

Measure allocations first, then look at the lines that allocate.

  1. Run the code under an allocation profiler (the Visual Studio .NET Object Allocation tool, dotnet-trace, or BenchmarkDotNet with [MemoryDiagnoser]). Boxing shows up as many small System.Int32, Guid or enum objects on the heap.
  2. Open the method in an IL viewer and search for the box instruction.
  3. Check the usual causes: ArrayList and Hashtable, parameters of type object or params object[], a struct used through an interface, and a struct key without IEquatable<T> in a dictionary.

The fix is nearly always generics: List<int>, a generic method, or IEquatable<T> on the struct.

code.title: var is checked at compile time, object needs a cast, dynamic is checked at run time

followUps:
No. var works only for local variables that are given a value on the same line, because the compiler needs that value to work out the type.

  • Allowed: var x = 5;, foreach (var item in list), using (var s = File.OpenRead(p)).
  • Not allowed: a field (private var total = 0;), a method parameter, a return type, or var x; with no value, and var x = null;.

For fields the nearest thing is target-typed new: private readonly List<int> _ids = new();. Lambda parameters can leave the type out (x => x * 2), but that is type inference, not var.

var hurts when the reader cannot see the type from the right-hand side of the line.

  • var result = service.Process(order); Is it a bool, an order, a task? Write the type or pick a better name.
  • var total = 0; is an int. If you meant decimal, later divisions silently drop the fraction.
  • var items = repo.GetAll(); hides whether you hold a List, an IEnumerable or an IQueryable, which changes where the query runs.

It is fine when the type is on the line already: var map = new Dictionary<string, int>(); or var user = (User)obj;.

Both find members at run time, but dynamic lets you write normal-looking C# and the runtime does the lookup, while reflection is an API you call by hand.

Use dynamic for COM or loose JSON, and reflection for tools that inspect types.

code.title: Strings never change; StringBuilder builds text in one buffer

followUps:
String interning means the runtime keeps one shared copy of each string literal in a table, so equal literals are the same object.

string a = "hi";
string b = "hi";                             // same object as a
string c = new string(new[] { 'h', 'i' });   // a new object
ReferenceEquals(a, b);                 // true
ReferenceEquals(a, c);                 // false
ReferenceEquals(a, string.Intern(c));  // true

Only literals (and constants joined at compile time) are interned automatically. Strings built at run time are not, unless you call string.Intern. Interned strings stay in memory for the life of the process, so do not intern user input. It is safe only because strings are immutable.

Yes, string is a reference type. == compares contents because the string class overloads the == operator to call string.Equals, which compares the characters one by one (an ordinal comparison).

One trap: operators are chosen at compile time from the declared type. If the variables are typed as object, you get reference comparison:

object a = "hi";
object b = new string(new[] { 'h', 'i' });
a == b;        // false: compares references
a.Equals(b);   // true: virtual call to string.Equals

Comparison is O(n) in the length, with a quick exit when both sides are the same object or have different lengths.

It keeps a buffer of characters and adds more room when the buffer is full, so most Append calls just copy characters into free space.

  • The default capacity is 16 characters.
  • In modern .NET the builder is a linked list of chunks. When the current chunk is full it adds a new chunk (about as big as everything so far, up to roughly 8,000 characters), so old text is not copied again.
  • ToString() copies all chunks once into the final string.

The effect is close to doubling: 16, 32, 64, and so on, so n appends cost O(n) overall. If you know the final size, pass it in (new StringBuilder(4096)) to skip the growth steps.

code.title: const, readonly and static readonly, and why a readonly list can still change

followUps:
No. A const must be a value the compiler can write straight into the compiled code, and that is only possible for numbers, bool, char, string, enum values and null.

public const int Max = 10;                              // fine
public const string Name = "orders";                    // fine
public const DateTime Start = new DateTime(2026, 1, 1); // compile error
public static readonly DateTime Start = new DateTime(2026, 1, 1);  // use this

static readonly is set when the type is first used and can hold any type. It also avoids the versioning trap of const: a public const is copied into every assembly that uses it, so changing it needs those assemblies to be rebuilt.

readonly struct means no field of the struct can change after the constructor finishes; the compiler rejects any member that tries.

public readonly struct Money
{
    public decimal Amount { get; }
    public Money(decimal amount) { Amount = amount; }
}

Two benefits:

  • Safety. A value like money or a date range cannot be changed by accident.
  • Speed. When a normal struct is reached through a readonly field or an in parameter, the compiler copies it before each method call in case the method changes it. For a readonly struct no such defensive copy is needed.

You can also mark single members readonly on a normal struct.

Because readonly protects the field, which holds a reference, and not the object that the reference points to.

private readonly List<string> _tags = new List<string>();
_tags.Add("vip");                 // allowed: same list, new content
_tags = new List<string>();       // compile error: the field is fixed

To stop changes to the content:

  • expose it as IReadOnlyList<string>, so callers get no Add (they could still cast back);
  • return _tags.AsReadOnly(), a wrapper that throws on changes;
  • use ImmutableList<string>, which truly cannot change: Add returns a new list.

code.title: Nullable value types: HasValue, ??, ?. and lifted maths

followUps:
! is the null-forgiving operator: it tells the compiler "I know this is not null, stop warning me". It does nothing at run time, so if you are wrong you still get a NullReferenceException.

string name = FindName(id)!;   // no warning, no check

It is acceptable when you know something the compiler cannot work out:

  • a value that was checked in another method, or by a framework (ModelState.IsValid passed, so a required field is set);
  • properties filled by a framework, such as public DbSet<Order> Orders { get; set; } = null!;;
  • tests that pass null! on purpose to check a guard clause.

If you write it often, fix the types or add a real check instead.

It returns 0, the default value of int, and it never throws.

int? a = null;
a.GetValueOrDefault();     // 0
a.GetValueOrDefault(18);   // 18
a ?? 18;                   // 18, the same thing
a.Value;                   // throws InvalidOperationException

For other types the default is the "all zeros" value: false for bool?, DateTime.MinValue for DateTime?. Take care that 0 is a sensible stand-in: for a missing discount it is, for a missing price or temperature it hides the fact that the data was absent.

Switch it on a little at a time, not for the whole solution in one go.

  1. Add <Nullable>enable</Nullable> to new projects straight away.
  2. In an old project, start with #nullable enable at the top of the files you touch, or set <Nullable>warnings</Nullable> to see the size of the problem.
  3. Work from the bottom up: shared models and libraries first, because their signatures tell every caller what may be null.
  4. Fix each warning properly: mark what really can be null with ?, and add guard clauses. Do not silence warnings with !.
  5. When a project is clean, enable it for the whole project and turn the nullable warnings into errors so it stays clean.

It changes no run-time behaviour, so it is safe to ship in small pull requests.

code.title: class, struct, record and record struct: copying and equality

followUps:
Because a struct is copied in full every time it is assigned, passed to a method or returned, so a big struct means a lot of copying.

A reference is 8 bytes on a 64-bit machine. A struct with four long fields is 32 bytes, and passing it through three method calls copies 96 bytes, where a class would copy 24. Microsoft's guideline is to keep structs around 16 bytes or less, immutable, and short-lived.

Good structs: a point, a money amount, a date range. If you need a large one, pass it with in or ref to avoid the copies, and make it a readonly struct. Structs kept in a list or as a field of a class are still stored inline, which is good for memory locality.

Only partly. A positional record class gets init-only properties, so those cannot be reassigned after creation, but nothing forces a record to be immutable.

record Person(string Name, int Age);          // Name, Age are init-only
record Basket(List<string> Items);            // Items.Add(...) still works
record Draft { public string Text { get; set; } }   // fully mutable
record struct Point(int X, int Y);            // X and Y are settable

So: the positional properties of a record class are fixed, but it is shallow (a list inside can still change), you may add set properties yourself, and a plain record struct is mutable unless you write readonly record struct.

Usually no. An entity is a thing with an identity (its key) that changes over time, and a record is built for values that are compared by content and copied instead of changed.

  • Equality. Two records with the same property values are equal, but two entities are the same only if they have the same key. Value equality over navigation properties can also be slow or loop.
  • Change tracking. EF Core tracks one object instance. order with { Status = "Paid" } makes a new, untracked object, so SaveChanges saves nothing.
  • Mutability. EF Core sets properties while loading and fixing up relationships.

Records are a good fit around the entity: DTOs, query projections, and value objects mapped as owned or complex types, such as Money or Address.

code.title: Flags enum, tuple return and pattern matching in one small program

followUps:
Because each power of two uses exactly one bit, so any combination of flags has its own unique number and can be taken apart again.

Read = 1 (001), Write = 2 (010), Delete = 4 (100)
Read | Write   = 3 (011)
Read | Delete  = 5 (101)

If you wrote Delete = 3, then 3 would mean both "Delete" and "Read and Write", and p.HasFlag(Delete) would be true for someone who only has Read and Write.

Write the values as 1 << 0, 1 << 1, 1 << 2 to avoid mistakes, keep None = 0, and add [Flags] so that ToString() prints Read, Write instead of 3. Named combinations such as All = 7 are fine.

ValueTuple is the modern one behind the (int, string) syntax: it is a struct with named elements. System.Tuple is the older class with Item1, Item2.

It throws a SwitchExpressionException at run time, because a switch expression must always produce a value.

string Name(int day) => day switch
{
    6 => "Saturday",
    7 => "Sunday"
};            // warning CS8509: not all values are handled
Name(3);      // throws SwitchExpressionException

The compiler warns you when it can see that some input is not covered. Fix it with a final discard arm: _ => "Weekday", or _ => throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(day)) when the value is truly invalid. An old switch statement with no matching case simply does nothing, which is the difference to remember.

code.title: Integer overflow with checked and unchecked, plus rounding and casting

followUps:
Mainly for speed, and because most integer maths in a program never comes near the limits.

  • A checked add needs an extra "did it overflow?" test after every operation. In tight loops over millions of numbers that cost is visible.
  • Some code wants the wrap-around on purpose: hash codes, checksums and random number generators.
  • It matches what C, C++ and Java do, so ported code behaves the same.

You can change the default for a whole project with <CheckForOverflowUnderflow>true</CheckForOverflowUnderflow> and then mark the few hot or hash-style spots unchecked. For money and counters that could be large, checked or a wider type (long, decimal) is the safe choice.

It returns 2, because Math.Round rounds a value that is exactly halfway to the nearest even number. This is called banker's rounding.

Math.Round(0.5) = 0    Math.Round(1.5) = 2
Math.Round(2.5) = 2    Math.Round(3.5) = 4

The reason is fairness over many values. Always rounding .5 upwards pushes totals up a little every time; rounding to even goes up half the time and down half the time, so the errors cancel out.

For the "school" rule, ask for it: Math.Round(2.5, MidpointRounding.AwayFromZero) gives 3. Also note that many decimals are not exact in double: Math.Round(2.675, 2) gives 2.67 because the stored value is slightly below 2.675. Use decimal for money.

The cast cuts the fraction off and gives 3, while Convert.ToInt32 rounds and gives 4.

Value(int)xConvert.ToInt32(x)
3.934

2.522 (rounds to even)
3.534
1e20a meaningless number, no errorthrows OverflowException

So the cast truncates towards zero and does not check the range (unless inside checked), and Convert uses banker's rounding and always checks. Use Math.Floor, Math.Ceiling or Math.Round first when you need a specific rule.

code.title: Comparing strings: ordinal, ignore case, and a case-insensitive dictionary

followUps:
It is the bug where code changes the case of text using Turkish rules and gets letters that no longer match the English ones.

Turkish has four letters where English has two: dotted i/İ and dotless ı/I. Under the tr-TR culture:

"file".ToUpper()   -> "FİLE"   (not "FILE")
"TITLE".ToLower()  -> "tıtle"  (not "title")

So input.ToUpper() == "FILE" works on your machine and fails on a server or phone set to Turkish. The fix is to never use culture rules for program text: compare with StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase, or use ToUpperInvariant() if you must change case.

Pass a comparer to the constructor: new Dictionary<string, int>(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase).

var stock = new Dictionary<string, int>(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase);
stock["Apple"] = 5;
stock["APPLE"] += 1;          // same key
Console.WriteLine(stock["apple"]);   // 6, and Count is 1

The comparer supplies both Equals and GetHashCode, so "Apple" and "APPLE" hash to the same bucket. This is better than calling ToLower() on every key, which creates a new string each time and is easy to forget in one place. HashSet<string>, Distinct, GroupBy and ToDictionary accept the same comparer. Lookups stay O(1) on average.

== on strings is ordinal: it compares the character codes one by one, and it is case-sensitive.

a.Contains(b), a.Replace(b, c)ordinal
a.CompareTo(b), string.Compare(a, b)current culture

Because the defaults are mixed, always pass a StringComparison to the methods that accept one. Code analysis rules CA1307 and CA1309 remind you.

code.title: ==, Equals, ReferenceEquals and GetHashCode on a class

followUps:
Hash-based collections stop finding your objects: Dictionary, HashSet, Distinct() and GroupBy() all give wrong answers.

These collections first use the hash code to pick a bucket and only then call Equals on the items in that bucket. Without your own GetHashCode, each object gets a hash based on its identity, so two equal objects go to different buckets and Equals is never even called.

var set = new HashSet<BadPoint> { new BadPoint(1, 2) };
set.Contains(new BadPoint(1, 2));   // false, although Equals says true

The rule: if a.Equals(b) then a.GetHashCode() == b.GetHashCode(). Build the hash from the same fields, for example HashCode.Combine(X, Y), and keep those fields unchanged while the object is a key.

IEquatable<T> gives your type a strongly typed Equals(T other), which is faster and safer than Equals(object).

  • No boxing for structs. Equals(object) has to box a struct argument on every call. With IEquatable<T> the generic collections call Equals(T) directly. For a struct used as a dictionary key this removes an allocation per lookup.
  • No cast and type check inside the method.
  • The collections look for it. EqualityComparer<T>.Default, used by List<T>.Contains, Dictionary, HashSet and LINQ, uses IEquatable<T> when it is present.

Still override Equals(object) and GetHashCode() and make all three agree. A record does all of this for you.

Yes. A hash code is only 32 bits, so there are about 4.3 billion possible values but an unlimited number of possible objects. Two different objects sharing a hash code is called a collision, and it is allowed.

The rule only goes one way: equal objects must have equal hash codes; unequal objects may have equal hash codes. That is why a dictionary always finishes with an Equals call to confirm the key.

Collisions cost speed, not correctness. With a good hash, a lookup checks one or two entries, which is O(1). If every key returned the same hash (return 1;), all entries would sit in one chain and each lookup would be O(n). So never use a hash code as a unique id or as proof that two things are equal.

code.title: ref, out, in, params, optional and named arguments

followUps:
Pass by value. Unless you write ref, out or in, the method gets its own copy of whatever the variable holds.

The confusion comes from what is copied:

  • for a value type (int, a struct) the copy is the data, so the caller never sees changes;
  • for a reference type (a class) the copy is the reference. Both copies point at one object, so p.Name = "Bo" is visible to the caller, but p = new Person() is not.

So "objects are passed by reference" is wrong; "references are passed by value" is right. Only ref and out give the method the caller's actual variable, which is why they must be written at the call site too: Swap(ref a, ref b).

No. void Read(ref int x) and void Read(out int x) in the same class give a compile error (CS0663).

The reason is that ref, out and in are the same thing to the runtime: all three pass the address of the variable. The differences (must be assigned before the call, must be assigned inside, read-only) are rules the C# compiler checks, so the two signatures are identical in the compiled code.

What you can do is overload between "by value" and "by reference":

void Read(int x) { }       // called with Read(n)
void Read(ref int x) { }   // called with Read(ref n)

That works because the caller has to write ref, so the compiler always knows which one is meant.

Callers keep using the old default until they are recompiled, because the default value is copied into the calling code at compile time.

Say your library has void Send(string msg, int retries = 3). An app that calls Send("hi") is compiled as Send("hi", 3). You ship a new library DLL with retries = 5. If the app only swaps the DLL and is not rebuilt, it still passes 3. Different apps now behave differently with the same library version, which is hard to debug.

Safer options for a public library:

  • use overloads: Send(string msg) => Send(msg, 5); so the default lives inside the library;
  • use null as the default and decide the real value inside the method;
  • put defaults in an options object.

code.title: int.Parse, int.TryParse and Convert.ToInt32 on good, bad and missing input

followUps:
Because 0 is a real, valid number, so "the value was missing" and "the value was zero" become impossible to tell apart.

Convert.ToInt32((string)null) returns 0 with no error. Examples of the damage:

  • a missing quantity in a request becomes an order for 0 items, which is saved instead of rejected;
  • a missing discountPercent column in an import becomes "no discount" for every customer;
  • a missing userId becomes user 0, which may be a real or special account.

For input from outside, use int.TryParse and treat failure as a validation error, or use int? so that "no value" stays null all the way to the database.

Tell the parser which culture the text is in; do not rely on the culture of the machine the code runs on.

var de = CultureInfo.GetCultureInfo("de-DE");
decimal a = decimal.Parse("1.234,56", de);                     // 1234.56
bool ok = decimal.TryParse("1234,56", NumberStyles.Number, de, out decimal b);

With no culture argument, Parse uses CultureInfo.CurrentCulture. On an en-US server "1,234" is read as one thousand two hundred and thirty-four, and on a German one as 1.234, so the same input gives different numbers.

Rules of thumb: text typed by a user is parsed with the user's culture; text between programs (JSON, CSV, config, URLs) is written and parsed with CultureInfo.InvariantCulture, which uses a dot.

It sets it to 0, the default value of int (in general, default(T) of the target type).

bool ok = int.TryParse("abc", out int n);   // ok = false, n = 0
bool ok2 = int.TryParse("0", out int m);    // ok2 = true, m = 0

So the number alone tells you nothing: you must look at the returned bool. A common bug is ignoring it:

int.TryParse(input, out int qty);   // result thrown away
Save(qty);                          // saves 0 for bad input

Use it in an if: if (!int.TryParse(input, out int qty)) return BadRequest();. The same holds for DateTime.TryParse (gives DateTime.MinValue) and Guid.TryParse (gives Guid.Empty).

code.title: Properties: auto, validated, private set, init, required and computed

followUps:
Because a property lets you change how the value is stored or checked later without changing any code that uses it.

  • Room to add logic. Today Price { get; set; }, tomorrow the setter rejects negatives or raises a change event. Callers do not change. Turning a field into a property later breaks compiled callers, because a field read and a method call are different instructions.
  • Different access for read and write: { get; private set; } or { get; init; }.
  • Interfaces can declare properties but not fields.
  • Frameworks expect them: model binding, System.Text.Json (by default), EF Core and UI data binding work on properties.
  • You can set a breakpoint on a setter to see who changes a value.

An auto property costs nothing: the JIT inlines it to a plain field access.

No. init only stops the property itself from being assigned again after the object is created; it says nothing about the object that the property points to.

class Order
{
    public string Id { get; init; }
    public List<string> Lines { get; init; } = new();
}
var o = new Order { Id = "A1" };
o.Id = "B2";          // compile error
o.Lines.Add("pen");   // allowed: the list itself is mutable

This is called shallow immutability. For deep immutability every level must be immutable too: use ImmutableList<T> or IReadOnlyList<T> for collections and init-only or readonly members in the nested types. Also note that reflection and serializers can still set init properties.

required (C# 11) makes the caller set the member in an object initializer, whichever constructor is used, unless that constructor is marked [SetsRequiredMembers].

class User
{
    public required string Email { get; init; }
    public User() { }
    [SetsRequiredMembers]
    public User(string email) { Email = email; }
}
new User { Email = "a@example.com" };  // ok
new User("a@example.com");             // ok: the attribute vouches for it
new User();                            // compile error: Email not set

The attribute is a promise the compiler does not verify, so make sure that constructor really sets every required member. The check happens at compile time only; System.Text.Json also honours required and throws when the JSON lacks the property.

code.title: Extension methods, a local function and expression-bodied members

followUps:
Yes. An extension method is a normal static method, so calling it on a null reference does not throw by itself; the null is simply passed in as the first argument.

string s = null;
s.IsBlank();                   // fine: compiles to StringExtensions.IsBlank(s)
s.Trim();                      // NullReferenceException: real instance method

That is why helpers like IsNullOrEmpty() can be written as extensions. It also means every extension method must decide what null means: either handle it, or fail clearly at the top with ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(source);. The LINQ operators do the second, so ((int[])null).Where(...) throws ArgumentNullException, not NullReferenceException.

Use a local function when you want a named helper inside one method, and a lambda when you need to hand a piece of code to something else as a value.

Typical uses: a local function for argument checks before an iterator or async body, or for a recursive walk; a lambda for list.Where(x => x > 5) or an event handler. Mark either one static if it should not capture anything.

If both namespaces are imported and the two methods have the same signature, the call does not compile: the compiler reports an ambiguous call (error CS0121).

Ways out:

  • call the one you want as a plain static method: TextHelpers.Truncate(s, 10);
  • remove one of the using lines in that file;
  • rename or delete the duplicate if you own it.

Two rules decide before ambiguity is reached. An instance method on the type always wins over any extension method, so if the type later gains a real method with that name, your extension silently stops being called. And an extension in a nearer scope (the current namespace) beats one brought in from a namespace further out.

Because the version that looks correct has a hidden hole: without volatile, a second thread can see a non-null field before the object behind it is fully built.

    lock (_gate)

return _instance;

Common mistakes:

  • leaving out volatile on _instance, so the write of the reference and the constructor's writes may be seen out of order on some CPUs;
  • dropping the second check, so two threads that both passed the first check each create an object;
  • locking on this or a type, which other code can also lock.

Use Lazy<T> or a static readonly field instead; the runtime guarantees both are created once.

The singleton keeps the first scoped object it was given for the whole life of the application. This is called a captive dependency.

A scoped service such as a DbContext is meant to live for one request. Held by a singleton, it is shared by every request and thread: it is not thread safe, its change tracker grows without limit, and it serves stale data.

ASP.NET Core checks this in the Development environment and throws "Cannot consume scoped service ... from singleton" at start-up. Fixes:

using var scope = _scopeFactory.CreateScope();
var db = scope.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<AppDbContext>();
  • or use IDbContextFactory<T>, or make the consumer scoped too.

code.title: Four pillars in one bank account example

Abstraction is about what you show: a simple view that leaves out detail. Encapsulation is about how you protect it: keeping the data private and letting it change only through methods that enforce the rules.

AbstractionEncapsulation

A car's pedals and wheel are the abstraction; the closed bonnet is the encapsulation. You can have one without the other: a class with all-public fields behind a nice interface is abstract but not encapsulated.

A classic one is a stack built by inheriting from a list, to "reuse" its storage.

class Stack<T> : List<T>
{
    public void Push(T item) => Add(item);
    public T Pop() { var x = this[Count - 1]; RemoveAt(Count - 1); return x; }
}
stack.Insert(0, item);   // legal, and breaks the stack

The stack inherits every public list method, so callers can insert in the middle, sort or clear it, and the "last in, first out" rule is gone. A stack is not a kind of list; it only uses one. The fix is composition: keep a private List<T> field and expose only Push, Pop and Peek.

In a real project, tell your own version: for example PremiumCustomer : Customer, which failed when customers could be upgraded and downgraded, so the tier became a field holding a pricing strategy.

Polymorphism lets you add a new behaviour by adding a new class, without editing the code that calls it. That is what "open for extension, closed for modification" asks for.

Without it, every new case edits an existing method:

if (type == "Savings") fee = 0;
else if (type == "Current") fee = 5;
else if (type == "Student") fee = 1;   // edit, retest, redeploy

With it, the caller is written once against the base type:

foreach (Account a in accounts) a.ChargeFee();

A new StudentAccount : Account with its own MonthlyFee() works straight away. The loop, its tests and every other account class are untouched, so the risk of breaking old behaviour is low. The same idea with interfaces and DI gives you pluggable payment providers, discount rules or exporters.

protected internal means protected or internal, the wider of the two. private protected means protected and internal, the narrower.

Use private protected for a helper in a base class that only your own subclasses in the same library should call, so that customers who inherit from your public class cannot reach it.

Public. A member written in an interface with no modifier is public, because an interface describes what callers are allowed to use.

interface IShape
{
    double Area();          // public, although it is not written
}
class Square : IShape
{
    public double Area() => 4;   // must be public here (or explicit)
}

Compare the other defaults: class and struct members are private; a top-level type is internal; enum members are always public. Since C# 8 an interface member that has a body may be given another modifier, such as private for a helper used by default methods, or protected, but the default stays public.

Let the test project see the internals with InternalsVisibleTo, or test the class through the public code that uses it.

<!-- in MyApp.csproj -->
<ItemGroup>
  <InternalsVisibleTo Include="MyApp.Tests" />
</ItemGroup>

The older form is an attribute in any source file: [assembly: InternalsVisibleTo("MyApp.Tests")]. After that the test assembly can create and call internal types as if they were public. Mocking libraries that generate proxies need the same line for DynamicProxyGenAssembly2.

Do not make the class public just for tests: that adds it to your supported API. And do not test private methods through reflection; test the behaviour they produce through a public or internal entry point.

code.title: Overloading is chosen at compile time, overriding at run time

followUps:
No. Two methods with the same name and the same parameters but different return types do not compile (error CS0111).

int Parse(string s) { ... }
long Parse(string s) { ... }   // error: already defined

Parse("42");        // which one? the result is not even used
var x = Parse("42");

The compiler chooses an overload by looking only at the arguments in the call, and a caller is free to ignore the return value, so the return type cannot help it decide. The signature that must be unique is the name plus the parameter types (and ref/out).

Ways round it: give the methods different names (ParseInt32, ParseInt64) or make the method generic: T Parse<T>(string s).

No. A static method belongs to the type, not to an object, so there is no object whose real type could decide which version runs. It cannot be marked virtual, abstract or override in a class.

A derived class can declare a static method with the same name, but that is hiding, not overriding:

class Base  { public static string Name() => "Base"; }
class Child : Base { public new static string Name() => "Child"; }
Base.Name();    // "Base"
Child.Name();   // "Child": chosen by the type you wrote, at compile time

One newer exception: since C# 11 an interface can declare static abstract or static virtual members, which implementing types supply and generic code calls as T.Method(). That is how generic maths works.

The compiler picks the overload whose parameter type is the most specific one that null can convert to, and reports an error if there is no single best one.

void Print(object o) { }
void Print(string s) { }
Print(null);            // calls Print(string): string is more specific than object

void Send(string s) { }
void Send(Uri u) { }
Send(null);             // error CS0121: ambiguous, string and Uri are unrelated
Send((string)null);     // fine: the cast tells the compiler which one

Value-type parameters such as int are not candidates, because null cannot be an int; int? is a candidate. To avoid surprises in your own APIs, do not offer overloads that differ only by unrelated reference types.

code.title: Constructors: chaining with this and base, a static constructor and a primary constructor

followUps:
The compiler adds a public constructor with no parameters that does nothing except call the base class constructor, so new Thing() still works.

class Thing { public int Size; }
var t = new Thing();      // works; Size is 0

All fields start at their default values (0, false, null) or at their field initialisers. Details worth knowing:

  • The free constructor disappears as soon as you write any constructor. Add Thing(int size) and new Thing() stops compiling, which can break serializers and EF Core, which often need a parameterless one.
  • For an abstract class the generated constructor is protected.
  • A struct can always be created with default, with all fields zeroed, without running any constructor.

Because the base constructor runs before the derived constructor body, so the overriding method runs on an object that is only half built.

class Base
{
    public Base() { Init(); }
    protected virtual void Init() { }
}
class Child : Base
{
    private readonly string _name;
    public Child(string name) { _name = name; }
    protected override void Init() => Console.WriteLine(_name.Length);  // _name is still null
}
new Child("x");   // NullReferenceException

The order is: derived field initialisers, base field initialisers, base constructor body, derived constructor body. C# dispatches to the override even inside the base constructor. Avoid it: pass what the base needs as constructor arguments, or use a separate Initialize() step or factory method called after construction. Analyzer rule CA2214 flags it.

On a record, each primary constructor parameter becomes a public property; on a class or struct, the parameters are only private variables that the class body can use.

record PersonR(string Name, int Age);
class  PersonC(string name, int age) { public string Name => name; }

var r = new PersonR("Asha", 30);
r.Name;                 // exists: public init-only property
var (n, a) = r;         // Deconstruct is generated too
var c = new PersonC("Asha", 30);
c.Age;                  // compile error: no such member

The record also uses those properties for Equals, GetHashCode, ToString and with. A class gets none of that. Also, class parameters are mutable captured variables: code inside the class can assign name = "x", and if you both capture a parameter and copy it into a property, the two can drift apart (the compiler warns).

code.title: Abstract class shares code and state; interface is a contract with an optional default method

followUps:
Yes. An abstract class can list an interface and either implement its members or pass them on to its children as abstract members.

interface IShape { double Area(); string Describe(); }

abstract class ShapeBase : IShape
{
    public abstract double Area();                      // children must write this
    public string Describe() => "Area " + Area();       // shared by all children
}
class Square : ShapeBase { public override double Area() => 4; }

Every interface member must be accounted for in the abstract class, even if only as an abstract declaration. This pairing is a very common design: the interface is what callers and tests depend on, and the abstract class is an optional "starter kit" that saves implementers from repeating the common code.

Because a class does not inherit members from the interfaces it implements. The default method stays a member of the interface, so it is visible only when the variable has the interface type.

interface ILogger { void Log(string m); void LogError(string m) => Log("ERROR: " + m); }
class ConsoleLogger : ILogger { public void Log(string m) { } }

var c = new ConsoleLogger();
c.LogError("x");               // compile error
((ILogger)c).LogError("x");    // works
ILogger l = c; l.LogError("x");   // works

This was a deliberate choice: adding a default method to an interface must never change or clash with the public surface of existing classes, and it avoids bringing multiple inheritance of implementation into classes. If the class wants the method on itself, it implements it as a normal public method, which then also replaces the default.

They let generic code call static members, such as operators, constants and factory methods, on a type parameter. They arrived in C# 11 and .NET 7.

static T Sum<T>(IEnumerable<T> items) where T : INumber<T>
{
    T total = T.Zero;                 // static member on T
    foreach (T x in items) total += x;   // operator + on T
    return total;
}
Sum(new[] { 1, 2, 3 });        // 6
Sum(new[] { 1.5m, 2.5m });     // 4.0

Uses:

  • Generic maths: one algorithm for int, double, decimal through INumber<T>;
  • Parsing: IParsable<T> gives T.Parse(text, null);
  • Factories: static abstract T Create(); so generic code can build a T without reflection.

code.title: virtual, override, new (hiding), abstract and sealed side by side

followUps:
You get a warning, not an error, and the method hides the base one, exactly as if you had written new.

  • CS0114 when the base method is virtual or abstract: "hides inherited member. To make the current member override that implementation, add the override keyword. Otherwise add the new keyword."
  • CS0108 when the base method is not virtual: "hides inherited member. Use the new keyword if hiding was intended."

The danger is that the code builds and seems fine, but calls through a base-type variable still run the base version:

Base b = new Child();
b.Who();    // "Base", not "Child"

Treat these two warnings as errors in the project file so a forgotten override cannot slip into production.

No. Writing override on a method whose base version is not virtual, abstract or override is a compile error (CS0506).

In C# methods are non-virtual by default (the opposite of Java), so the base class author must opt in. Your options when the base method is not virtual:

  • Hide it with new. This only affects calls made through the derived type, so it is rarely what you want.
  • Change the base class to mark the method virtual, if you own it.
  • Wrap instead of inherit: hold the object in a field and expose your own method (composition, a decorator).
  • Depend on an interface that both the original and your version implement.

For tests, this is why mocking libraries can only fake virtual members and interfaces.

Because the JIT compiler then knows that no subclass can exist, so it can turn virtual calls into direct calls and often inline them.

  • Devirtualisation. A virtual call reads the object's method table and jumps through it. If the variable's type is sealed, the target is known at compile time, so the JIT calls it directly and can inline a small method.
  • Cheaper type checks. obj is Leaf for a sealed class is one pointer comparison; for an unsealed class the runtime may have to walk up the inheritance chain.
  • Casting arrays and some span operations skip covariance checks.

The gain is small per call and matters only in hot paths. The bigger reason to seal is design: you promise less, so you can change the class later. Many teams seal by default (analyzer CA1852 suggests it).

code.title: Three kinds of polymorphism: overloads, virtual methods and generics

Compile-time. An overloaded operator is a static method, and the compiler chooses which one to call from the declared types of the two operands.

object a = "hi";
object b = new string(new[] { 'h', 'i' });
a == b;                    // false: the compiler picked object's ==, a reference comparison
(string)a == (string)b;    // true: now it picks string's ==

The objects are the same in both lines; only the variable types changed, and so did the result. That is the proof that operators are not virtual. If you want comparison to follow the real type, call the virtual Equals method. (Using dynamic operands delays the choice to run time, but that is the dynamic binder at work, not operator overloading itself.)

Virtual methods make it easy to add a new type; pattern matching makes it easy to add a new operation. Choose by which of the two you expect to grow.

Virtual methodsPattern matching
Add a type (Triangle)one new classfind and edit every switch

{
