    Square q => q.Side * q.Side,
    _ => throw new NotSupportedException()
};

Pattern matching suits plain data such as DTOs, messages and syntax trees.

Double dispatch means choosing the method to run from the real types of two objects, not one.

A C# virtual call uses only the type of the object before the dot (single dispatch). Arguments are matched at compile time by their declared types. So collide(Shape a, Shape b) cannot pick "circle hits square" by itself.

The standard solution is the visitor pattern, which makes two virtual calls in a row:

abstract class Shape { public abstract void Accept(IVisitor v); }
class Circle : Shape { public override void Accept(IVisitor v) => v.Visit(this); }
interface IVisitor { void Visit(Circle c); void Visit(Square s); }

Call 1 (shape.Accept) resolves the shape's type; inside it, this is a Circle, so call 2 picks Visit(Circle) on the visitor's real type. Alternatives: a switch on a tuple of the two objects, or dynamic.

code.title: One base class only; interfaces with the same method are kept apart

followUps:
C++ allows multiple inheritance and gives the programmer two tools: qualifying the call with the base class name, and virtual inheritance.

  • Without virtual inheritance, D : B, C where both derive from A contains two copies of A. A plain d.value or d.f() is a compile error for being ambiguous; you must write d.B::f() or d.C::f().
  • With virtual inheritance (class B : virtual public A, same for C), D holds one shared A. If both B and C override the same virtual function, D must override it too.

It works, but it adds cost (extra pointers), tricky constructor order and code that is hard to read. The designers of C# and Java chose to leave it out and offer interfaces instead.

No. A struct cannot inherit from another struct or from a class, and nothing can inherit from a struct.

Every struct is implicitly sealed and derives from System.ValueType (which derives from object). The reason is how values are stored: a struct variable holds the data itself in a fixed-size space with no type header. If a bigger derived struct could be assigned to it, the extra fields would have nowhere to go and would be cut off.

What a struct can do:

  • implement any number of interfaces: struct Money : IEquatable<Money>, IComparable<Money>;
  • override ToString, Equals and GetHashCode from object;
  • reuse another struct by holding it as a field (composition).

It depends on whether the two defaults are for two separate methods or for the same one.

  • Unrelated interfaces, IA.Run() and IB.Run(), each with a default: no conflict. They are two different members and neither appears on the class. ((IA)x).Run() runs one and ((IB)x).Run() runs the other.
  • A real diamond, where IB and IC both re-implement IA.Run() and a class implements both: compile error CS8705, "does not have a most specific implementation". The compiler refuses to guess.

The fix is for the class to implement the method itself:

class D : IB, IC
{
    public void Run() { /* D decides */ }
}

A class's own implementation always beats any interface default, so the ambiguity is gone.

code.title: Explicit interface implementation: same method name, two meanings, and a hidden member

followUps:
No. An explicit interface member takes no access modifier at all; writing public on it is a compile error (CS0106).

class Greeter : IEnglish
{
    string IEnglish.Greet() => "Hello";          // correct
    public string IEnglish.Greet() => "Hello";   // error CS0106
}

Its visibility is special: it cannot be called through a variable of the class type, not even from inside the class with this.Greet(), but anyone who holds the object as the interface type can call it. So it is "private to the class, public through the interface". If you also want it on the class, add a normal public method and have the explicit one call it.

An explicit member cannot be virtual, so a derived class cannot override it directly. There are two ways to change the behaviour.

1. Let the explicit member call a protected virtual method (the cleaner way, when you own the base class):

class Base : IGreeter
{
    string IGreeter.Greet() => GreetCore();
    protected virtual string GreetCore() => "Hello";
}
class Child : Base { protected override string GreetCore() => "Hi"; }

2. Re-implement the interface in the derived class by listing it again:

class Child : Base, IGreeter
{
    string IGreeter.Greet() => "Hi";
}

With option 2 a call through IGreeter on a Child object runs the child's version, but the child cannot call the base version, since it is not reachable through base.

In many of the collection and primitive types, mostly to hide members that make no sense on the concrete type.

  • Arrays implement IList<T>, but Add and Remove are explicit and throw NotSupportedException, because an array has a fixed size. You never see array.Add.
  • List<T> implements the old non-generic IEnumerable.GetEnumerator() and ICollection<T>.IsReadOnly explicitly, so the class shows only the fast generic GetEnumerator().
  • Dictionary<TKey, TValue> hides ICollection<KeyValuePair<..>>.Add(pair), so you use Add(key, value).
  • int, double and the other primitives implement IConvertible explicitly; you call Convert.ToDouble(x) instead of x.ToDouble(...).

Yes. sealed only stops other classes from inheriting from this class; it puts no limit on what the class itself inherits or implements.

public sealed class Money : IEquatable<Money>, IComparable<Money>
{
    public decimal Amount { get; }
    public Money(decimal amount) { Amount = amount; }
    public bool Equals(Money other) => other != null && Amount == other.Amount;
    public int CompareTo(Money other) => Amount.CompareTo(other.Amount);
}

The best-known example is string: it is sealed and implements IComparable, IEnumerable<char>, IEquatable<string> and more. Sealed classes that implement interfaces are the normal shape for services registered in dependency injection.

It can have a static constructor, but not an instance constructor, because no object of a static class is ever created.

static class Lookup
{
    public static readonly Dictionary<string, int> Codes;
    static Lookup()            // no access modifier, no parameters
    {
        Codes = new Dictionary<string, int> { ["GB"] = 44, ["IN"] = 91 };
    }
}

The runtime calls the static constructor once, automatically, before the first member of the class is used, and it does so in a thread-safe way. You cannot call it yourself. If it throws, the type is unusable for the rest of the process: every later use throws TypeInitializationException, so keep the work in it small and safe.

To take control of how, and how many, objects of the class are created.

  • Singleton: only the class itself can call new, so it can guarantee one instance.
  • Factory methods: creation goes through named static methods that can validate, cache or return a subtype.
public sealed class Email
{
    public string Value { get; }
    private Email(string value) { Value = value; }
    public static Email Parse(string text)
    {
        if (!text.Contains("@")) throw new FormatException("Not an email");
        return new Email(text.Trim().ToLowerInvariant());
    }
}
  • Stopping inheritance from outside: a derived class must call a base constructor, and it cannot reach a private one (only nested classes can).
  • Holders of constants or static helpers in old code; today mark those static class.

code.title: Inheritance explosion versus composition with a strategy

followUps:
Give a real story in three parts: the problem, the change, the result. Here is a model answer to adapt.

"We had ReportBase with PdfReport and ExcelReport. Then customers wanted a daily and a monthly variant of each, then a version emailed or saved to disk. We reached eight subclasses with copied code, and a bug fix had to be repeated in each. I split it into a ReportBuilder that takes an IFormatter (PDF, Excel) and an IDelivery (email, disk) through its constructor. The eight classes became four small ones, tests used fakes for delivery, and a new format took one class and one DI registration."

Say what you measured: fewer classes, fewer duplicate fixes, faster tests.

The Liskov substitution principle says: code that works with a base type must still work correctly when you hand it any subtype. If a subclass cannot keep that promise, inheritance is the wrong tool.

The classic failure is Square : Rectangle. Code that sets Width = 4; Height = 5; and expects an area of 20 gets 25 from a square, because setting one side changes the other.

Check a subclass with these questions:

  • Does it throw NotSupportedException for an inherited method?
  • Does it need stricter inputs or give weaker results than the base?
  • Does a caller have to check the type before using it?

One "yes" means the "is-a" claim is false for behaviour, so use composition or a smaller interface.

Composition costs you more small pieces and more wiring, and you give up some automatic reuse.

  • More types and indirection. A reader must follow calls through interfaces to see what really runs.
  • Forwarding code. To expose a helper's method you write a one-line method that calls it; inheritance gives that for free.
  • Wiring. Someone must create and connect the parts: a constructor with several parameters, or a DI container.
  • Hard to reuse protected state. The part cannot reach the owner's internals unless you pass them in.

Keep inheritance for a stable, true "is-a" relationship with shared state, such as Exception types or framework base classes (ControllerBase, BackgroundService). Use composition for everything that is "has-a" or "uses".

code.title: Testing through an interface with a hand-written fake clock and fake repository

followUps:
All three replace a real dependency in a test; they differ in how much they do and what you check.

KindWhat it doesYou check
Stubreturns fixed answersthe result of the code under test
Fakea simple working version, e.g. an in-memory repositorythe state it holds afterwards
Mockrecords the calls it receivedthat the right calls were made, e.g. "Send was called once"

The FakeClock above is a stub, and FakeRepo is a fake. Prefer stubs and fakes: they test the outcome. Use a mock only when the call itself is the outcome (an email must be sent), because mock-heavy tests break whenever the internal steps change.

Do not call it directly; hide it behind a small clock interface, or use TimeProvider, which has been in .NET since version 8.

class Trial(TimeProvider time)
{
    public bool Expired(DateTime end) => time.GetUtcNow().UtcDateTime > end;
}
// test
var fake = new FakeTimeProvider(new DateTimeOffset(2026, 5, 4, 0, 0, 0, TimeSpan.Zero));
fake.Advance(TimeSpan.FromDays(31));

TimeProvider.System is used in production, and FakeTimeProvider (a test package) lets a test set and move the time. It also controls timers and delays, so retry and timeout code can be tested without waiting. Before .NET 8, write your own IClock.

An interface is over-engineering when it has one implementation, you will never replace it, and nothing in the test needs to fake it.

  • Pure logic with no outside effects (a price calculator, a validator) can be tested directly. Wrapping it in IPriceCalculator only adds a file.
  • Interfaces that copy a class one-for-one, such as IFoo next to Foo and nothing else, add no abstraction.
  • DTOs, records and plain data classes do not need one.

Add an interface at a real boundary: the database, HTTP calls, the file system, the clock, message queues, or a place where you expect several implementations (payment providers). A good test is: "Would I fake this in a unit test?" If not, wait until you need it.

code.title: Covariance and contravariance with IEnumerable, Action and arrays

followUps:
Because covariance works by treating a reference to a child as a reference to its parent, which only works when both have the same shape in memory. An int is stored as raw 4 bytes and an object as a pointer.

Converting IEnumerable<int> to IEnumerable<object> would need every item to be boxed into a new object as it is read. Variance is only allowed when the conversion keeps the same object identity, with no change to the data.

The workaround is to convert explicitly: ints.Cast<object>() or ints.Select(i => (object)i). Both box each item, O(n) time.

The same limit applies to a struct: IEnumerable<MyStruct> is not an IEnumerable<IMyInterface>.

Both. Func<in T, out TResult> is contravariant in its input type and covariant in its result type.

Func<Animal, Cat> f = a => new Cat();
Func<Cat, Animal> g = f;   // legal
// takes a Cat (f accepts any Animal, so a Cat is fine)
// returns an Animal (f returns a Cat, which is an Animal)

The rule of thumb: the function may ask for less than promised (accept a wider input) and give back more than promised (return a narrower output). Action<in T> is contravariant, IEnumerable<out T> and IReadOnlyList<out T> are covariant, and IComparer<in T> is contravariant.

Answer with a real case or, if you have none, a plausible one and say it is an example. A good one is a handler interface:

public interface IEventHandler<in TEvent>
{
    Task Handle(TEvent e);
}
class LogAllHandler : IEventHandler<IDomainEvent> { ... }
IEventHandler<OrderPlaced> h = new LogAllHandler();  // contravariance

One handler for the base event type can be registered wherever a handler for a specific event is required. Another is a repository reader: interface IReader<out T> { T Get(int id); }, so an IReader<Cat> serves as an IReader<Animal>.

The restriction to remember: an out parameter can appear only in return positions, and an in parameter only in input positions. Also, interfaces and delegates can be variant; classes cannot.

code.title: Array, List<T> and ArrayList: size, growth and boxing

followUps:
Length is for arrays, Count is for collections, and Count() is a LINQ method that works on any sequence.

  • array.Length: a stored field, O(1).
  • list.Count, dictionary.Count: a stored property, O(1).
  • sequence.Count(): if the object is an ICollection it reads its Count (O(1)). On a lazy sequence such as a Where result or a database query, it must walk every item (O(n)).

So list.Count() works but adds a type check; list.Count > 0 is the right call. For "is there any?", use Any(), which stops at the first item.

Because the list keeps its items in one continuous block, so inserting at the start means moving every other item one place to the right.

For a list of 1,000,000 items, Insert(0, x) copies 1,000,000 references or values each time, so adding n items to the front costs O(n²) in total. Inserting at the end is O(1) amortised because nothing moves; RemoveAt(0) has the same shifting problem.

Better options:

  • Queue<T> when you add at one end and remove at the other;
  • LinkedList<T> if you really need fast inserts at both ends (it uses more memory and is slower to scan);
  • add at the end and read the list in reverse, or call Reverse() once.

Choose an array when the size is known and will not change, or when speed and memory matter most.

  • Fixed data: a lookup table, the days of the week, a buffer of 4096 bytes.
  • Performance: no wrapper object, no version checks, and the JIT can remove bounds checks in simple loops. byte[] is also the type that I/O, hashing and encoding methods expect.
  • Multi-dimensional data: int[,] or jagged int[][] for grids.
  • Span and memory: Span<T> slices of arrays avoid copying.
  • Params and interop: params string[], native calls.

Use List<T> for everything that grows or shrinks. If you know the final size, pass it as the capacity to avoid regrowing.

code.title: Generic class, generic method and constraints

followUps:
default(T) is the "empty" starting value of the type: 0 for numbers, false for bool, null for any class, and a struct with all fields zeroed.

T Last<T>(List<T> xs) => xs.Count == 0 ? default : xs[^1];
Last(new List<int>());      // 0
Last(new List<string>());   // null

You use it when generic code must return or store "no value" and does not know what T is. Take care: for int the result 0 looks like real data. If the caller must tell "none" apart, return bool TryGet(out T value) or T?. Since C# 7.1 you may write plain default when the type can be inferred.

Because the compiler does not know that T has a public constructor with no parameters. T might be int (which does), string (which has none), or an abstract class (which cannot be created).

T Make<T>() => new T();                       // error CS0304
T Make<T>() where T : new() => new T();       // fine

The new() constraint is a promise that every type used for T has an accessible parameterless constructor, and the compiler checks it at each call site. The constraint is limited to parameterless constructors. For constructors with arguments, pass a factory Func<T> or a Func<int, T>, or use static abstract interface members (C# 11).

With a generic class the type parameter is fixed for the whole object, and with a generic method it is chosen for each call.

class Box<T>  { T value; T Get() => value; }       // new Box<int>(), T is fixed inside
static class Util
{
    public static T First<T>(IEnumerable<T> xs) => xs.First();
}
Util.First(new[] { 1, 2 });      // T = int here
Util.First(new[] { "a" });       // T = string here, same class

Use a generic class when several members share the same T (a stack, a repository). Use a generic method for a stand-alone operation. The compiler usually infers T from the arguments, so you rarely write First<int>(...). A generic class can also contain generic methods with their own type parameters.

code.title: Choosing a collection: timing List, HashSet and Dictionary lookups

followUps:
Because List.Contains compares the target with items one by one until it finds a match, which is O(n), while HashSet.Contains turns the target into a hash code and jumps straight to one bucket, which is O(1) on average.

For a collection of 1,000,000 items, a missing value costs one million comparisons in the list and about one hash plus one or two comparisons in the set. In a loop that checks 1,000 values the list does about a billion comparisons, and the set about a thousand.

The set pays with extra memory (the bucket table) and no order or index. If you test membership more than a few times, build a HashSet once. For under about ten items a list is just as fast.

A sorted collection wins when you need the items in order, or need ranges and neighbours, which a hash table cannot give.

  • Ordered walking: SortedDictionary or SortedSet enumerate keys in order with no sort step.
  • Range and nearest queries: SortedSet<T>.GetViewBetween(a, b), Min and Max in O(log n).
  • No good hash: keys that are easy to compare but hard to hash.
  • Predictable cost: every operation is O(log n); a hash table can stall during a resize.
  • Small or read-mostly data: a sorted array with Array.BinarySearch uses less memory.

For pure key lookup a dictionary is faster: O(1) against O(log n).

Yes, as long as nobody is writing at the same time. Many threads may read a Dictionary at once if no thread adds, removes or changes an item while they do.

Reads do not change the internal arrays, so they do not disturb each other. The danger is a write during a read: a resize can move entries to a new array, and a reader can then loop forever, skip a key, or throw. Two writers can corrupt the structure.

Options:

  • build it once at start-up, never change it, and share it (or wrap it as FrozenDictionary, .NET 8, which is made for this);
  • ConcurrentDictionary when threads also write;
  • a lock around every access, or ImmutableDictionary with an atomic swap of the whole reference.

code.title: IEnumerable runs in memory, IQueryable builds a query: a fake database shows the difference

followUps:
AsEnumerable() changes the compile-time type of a query to IEnumerable<T>, so everything written after it runs in your program's memory instead of in the database.

var rows = db.Orders
    .Where(o => o.Total > 100)         // translated to SQL
    .AsEnumerable()                     // SQL runs here, rows come back
    .Where(o => MyLocalRule(o));        // C# method the database cannot run

It is useful when part of the filter calls a method that EF cannot translate. Put as much as you can before it, because every row after that point is downloaded. Used too early it turns a small query into loading a whole table. ToList() also ends the SQL part, but it copies everything into a list immediately.

It is debatable because a returned IQueryable lets callers keep building the SQL, which leaks the database into places that should not know about it.

  • For: callers can add their own filter, sort and paging, and only one query runs. You avoid writing a repository method for each combination.
  • Against: the repository no longer controls what SQL runs. A caller can add a filter that cannot be translated, call it after the context is disposed, trigger N+1 queries, or depend on EF-specific behaviour. Unit tests with in-memory lists behave differently from a real provider.

A common compromise: return IEnumerable or a list from specific, well-named methods (GetOpenOrders(page)) and, for generic needs, use a specification object or use the DbContext directly in query handlers, as EF Core already is a repository and unit of work.

An IEnumerable<T> is the sequence you can loop over; an IEnumerator<T> is the cursor that does the looping and remembers where you are.

foreach (var x in seq) { ... }
// is roughly
using (var e = seq.GetEnumerator())
    while (e.MoveNext()) { var x = e.Current; ... }

The enumerable has one method, GetEnumerator(), and can give a new cursor each time, so two loops over the same list do not disturb each other. The enumerator has MoveNext(), Current and Reset(), and it is disposable. Because a cursor holds state, List<T>.Enumerator is a struct (no allocation), and changing the list while a cursor is open throws "Collection was modified".

code.title: LINQ: deferred execution, Where, GroupBy, Join and SelectMany

followUps:
Select turns each item into one new item, so the output has the same length. SelectMany turns each item into a list of items and joins all those lists into one flat result.

var orders = new[] { new { Id = 1, Lines = new[] { "pen", "ink" } },
                     new { Id = 2, Lines = new[] { "pad" } } };
orders.Select(o => o.Lines);        // 2 items, each an array: [pen,ink], [pad]
orders.SelectMany(o => o.Lines);    // 3 items: pen, ink, pad

Use SelectMany for one-to-many: all lines of all orders, all words of all sentences. A second overload also gives you the parent: SelectMany(o => o.Lines, (o, line) => o.Id + ":" + line). It is the same as a nested foreach.

Operators that must read the whole sequence at once, or that return a single value or a collection, run immediately. The ones that return another sequence and can yield item by item are deferred.

  • Immediate, single value: Count, Sum, Min, Max, Average, First, Single, Any, All, Contains, Aggregate.
  • Immediate, makes a collection: ToList, ToArray, ToDictionary, ToHashSet.
  • Deferred: Where, Select, SelectMany, Take, Skip, Concat, Zip, OrderBy, GroupBy, Join, Distinct.

A subtle one: OrderBy and GroupBy are deferred, but once you read their first item they read the whole source.

Group the matching rows of the other list under each left item, then use DefaultIfEmpty() so a left item with no match still appears once.

var q = from d in depts
        join e in staff on d.Id equals e.DeptId into matches
        from m in matches.DefaultIfEmpty()
        select new { d.Title, Person = m == null ? "(nobody)" : m.Name };
// Eng/Asha, Eng/Chen, Ops/Ben, HR/(nobody)

Without DefaultIfEmpty() you get an inner join and HR disappears. In method syntax: GroupJoin then SelectMany. .NET 10 adds a built-in LeftJoin operator. In EF Core this translates to a SQL LEFT JOIN, or you can use a navigation property and Include.

code.title: Any versus Count, Where before OrderBy, and ToList in the wrong place

followUps:
No. It is O(1) when the sequence already knows its size, and O(n) when it has to walk the items to count them.

  • On a List<T>, array, HashSet or Dictionary, Count() checks for ICollection and reads the stored Count: O(1). Since .NET 6 some other sources, such as Range and Repeat, can do the same.
  • On a Where result, a yield iterator or a file reader, it loops through everything: O(n).
  • Count(x => ...) with a predicate is always O(n).
  • On IQueryable it becomes a SQL COUNT(*), which is fast but still scans the matching rows.

For "any items?" use Any(). To only know whether there are at least n, use Take(n).Count() or .NET's TryGetNonEnumeratedCount.

The N+1 problem is when one query loads a list of n rows and then your code runs one more query for each row, so n + 1 database trips instead of one or two.

var orders = db.Orders.ToList();               // 1 query
foreach (var o in orders)
    Console.WriteLine(o.Customer.Name);        // +1 query per order, with lazy loading

With 1,000 orders that is 1,001 round trips; at 2 ms each, about 2 seconds instead of a few milliseconds. Fixes:

  • Include(o => o.Customer), which adds a join or a second batched query;
  • a projection: Select(o => new { o.Id, CustomerName = o.Customer.Name }), which fetches only the needed columns;
  • turn lazy loading off so mistakes show up as errors rather than slowness.

Log the SQL (LogTo) in development to notice repeats.

Replace LINQ with a plain loop in a measured hot path, where the allocations or delegate calls matter, or when the logic is clearer as steps.

  • Hot paths: each lambda is a delegate call, each operator creates an iterator object, and closures allocate. Over millions of calls this shows in a profiler. A for loop over an array or Span<T> has none of that.
  • Single pass for several results: computing min, max and sum in one loop instead of three LINQ calls that walk the data three times.
  • Complex state: loops with early exits, counters and mutable state read better than a long chain.

Do not do it without measuring (BenchmarkDotNet). For normal business code, LINQ's clarity is worth more than the few nanoseconds.

code.title: Writing LINQ operators with yield return: Where, Take and Select

followUps:
The compiler turns the method into a hidden class that implements IEnumerator<T> as a state machine. The method body is cut at each yield return, and the position is stored in a field.

// roughly generated for a method with two yields
bool MoveNext()
{
    switch (state)
    {
        case 0: state = 1; Current = 1; return true;    // first yield
        case 1: state = 2; Current = 2; return true;    // second yield
        default: return false;
    }
}

Your local variables and parameters become fields of that class, which is how they survive between calls. Nothing runs when you call the method; the code up to the first yield return runs on the first MoveNext(). A foreach over it that ends early disposes the iterator, which runs any finally blocks.

Both are an extension method on IEnumerable<T> with a loop and yield return.

static IEnumerable<TOut> MySelect<T, TOut>(this IEnumerable<T> s, Func<T, TOut> f)
{
    foreach (var x in s) yield return f(x);
}
static IEnumerable<T> MyTake<T>(this IEnumerable<T> s, int n)
{
    if (n <= 0) yield break;
    int i = 0;
    foreach (var x in s) { yield return x; if (++i == n) yield break; }
}

The detail interviewers look for in Take is the check after the yield: stopping as soon as n items were given, so the source is not asked for item n+1. Add a null check too; because the iterator is lazy, an argument check inside it fires late, so real code checks in a normal wrapper method that calls a private iterator.

IAsyncEnumerable<T> is a sequence whose items arrive asynchronously, so you can await between items. You read it with await foreach and write it with async plus yield return.

async IAsyncEnumerable<Order> ReadOrders([EnumeratorCancellation] CancellationToken ct = default)
{
    while (await reader.ReadAsync(ct))
        yield return Map(reader);
}
await foreach (var o in ReadOrders(ct)) Process(o);

Use it when each item needs I/O to produce: streaming rows from a database, pages of an API, lines from a network stream, messages from a channel. Memory stays small because you hold one item at a time, and the caller can start working before the last one arrives. ASP.NET Core can return it directly and writes the JSON as a stream.

code.title: A tiny hash table: buckets, collisions and why bad hashes are slow

followUps:
Every key lands in the same bucket, so the dictionary becomes one long linked list and each lookup is O(n) instead of O(1).

With 2,000 keys and a hash that returns 1, a lookup compares against about half the keys on average, so reading all of them takes about two million comparisons instead of two thousand. The program above shows the effect.

This is also a security issue: if an attacker can pick keys that collide (for example query-string names), they can make a server spend minutes on a small request. This is a "hash flooding" attack. .NET defends against it with a randomised string hash, and .NET Core 3.0 onwards switches to a safer comparer after many collisions in a string-keyed dictionary.

Because .NET deliberately randomises string hashing: each process starts with a new random seed, so the same string gets a different hash in each run.

The reason is the hash-flooding attack above. If hashes were the same on every run, an attacker could work out a list of strings that collide and send them to your server. A secret per-process seed makes that impossible.

What this means for you:

  • Never store string.GetHashCode() in a database, file or cache key, or send it to another service; it is only valid inside one running process.
  • Do not rely on Dictionary or HashSet enumeration order either.
  • For a stable hash use SHA-256 or System.IO.Hashing.XxHash3 over the UTF-8 bytes.

ConcurrentDictionary is safe for many threads to read and write at once, and it does this by splitting the table into several locks instead of using one.

  • Reads take no lock at all.
  • Writes lock only one stripe of buckets, so writers to different keys rarely wait for each other.
  • Atomic helpers: GetOrAdd and AddOrUpdate do the check and the change as one step.
var counts = new ConcurrentDictionary<string, int>();
counts.AddOrUpdate("a", 1, (k, old) => old + 1);

One trap: the factory function you pass to GetOrAdd may run more than once if two threads race, and only one result is kept. So the factory must have no side effects, or wrap the value in Lazy<T>. It is slower than a plain Dictionary for single-threaded use.

code.title: Delegates, Func, Action, Predicate and a multicast delegate

followUps:
A multicast delegate is a delegate that holds a list of methods, and calling it calls every method in the list in the order they were added.

Action<string> log = Console.WriteLine;
log += s => File.AppendAllText("log.txt", s);
log("hello");        // writes to both
log -= someHandler;  // remove one

Details: += builds a new delegate each time (delegates are immutable); if one handler throws, the remaining ones do not run; for a non-void delegate you get only the last return value; and GetInvocationList() lets you call the handlers one by one to catch errors separately. Events are built on this.

Both pass behaviour into a method, but a delegate is one method with a shape, while an interface is a named contract that can have several methods and state.

// delegate: lightweight
void Run(Func<int, bool> rule) { ... }
Run(n => n > 5);

// interface: more ceremony, more room
interface IRule { bool Check(int n); string Name { get; } }
void Run(IRule rule) { ... }

Choose a delegate for a single operation that is likely to be a small lambda (callbacks, Where, Select, retry actions). Choose an interface when the behaviour has several members, needs its own state or dependencies, must be registered in DI, or needs a name for logging and testing. A class implementing a one-method interface and a lambda are interchangeable in most designs.

Invoke is the method that actually calls the delegate; d(x) is a shorthand that the compiler turns into d.Invoke(x). The form d?.Invoke(x) checks for null first and calls only if there are handlers.

Action<string> d = null;
d("x");           // NullReferenceException
d?.Invoke("x");   // does nothing, no exception

The ?. operator has no short form with brackets, which is the reason to write Invoke out. It is also thread safe: it reads the delegate field once into a temporary, so another thread removing the last handler between the check and the call cannot cause a null reference. That is why MyEvent?.Invoke(this, e) is the standard way to raise an event.

code.title: Events and publish/subscribe with EventHandler<T>

followUps:
It reads the event field once, so another thread cannot remove the last subscriber between your null check and the call.

// risky
if (OrderPlaced != null)       // 1. not null
    OrderPlaced(this, e);      // 2. but now null? NullReferenceException

// safe
OrderPlaced?.Invoke(this, e);  // reads the field once into a temporary

Delegates are immutable. A -= on another thread swaps the field for a new delegate (or null), but the copy that ?.Invoke already holds still points at the old list. The result is that the handler might still run once after being removed, which is a normal race and rarely matters. It is also shorter to write.

Keep the lambda in a variable and use that variable for both the subscribe and the unsubscribe. A new lambda written a second time is a different object, so removing it does nothing.

EventHandler h = (s, e) => Console.WriteLine("hi");
button.Click += h;
button.Click -= h;                           // works

button.Click += (s, e) => Console.WriteLine("hi");
button.Click -= (s, e) => Console.WriteLine("hi");   // does nothing: different object

A handler can also unsubscribe itself by naming itself: declare EventHandler h = null; h = (s, e) => { ...; button.Click -= h; };. Or avoid manual events, and use IObservable subscriptions, which return an IDisposable to cancel.

The weak event pattern lets a subscriber be garbage collected even if it forgot to unsubscribe, because the publisher holds only a weak reference to it.

With a normal event, the publisher's delegate list points at the subscriber, so a long-lived publisher (a static event, a singleton service) keeps every subscriber alive for ever. In a UI app that is a classic memory leak: closed windows stay in memory and keep reacting to events.

Options:

  • Unsubscribe in Dispose or on close; the simplest fix.
  • WPF's WeakEventManager or WeakReference-based wrappers.
  • Messenger classes (the community toolkit's WeakReferenceMessenger) that hold weak references by design.

Use it only when subscriber lifetime is shorter than publisher lifetime and cannot be managed.

code.title: Closures capture variables, not values: the loop trap

followUps:
It moves each captured variable out of the stack frame into a hidden helper class on the heap, and makes the lambda a method of that class.

// you write
int count = 0;
Func<int> next = () => ++count;

// compiler makes (roughly)
class Display { public int count; public int Lambda() => ++this.count; }
var d = new Display(); d.count = 0;
Func<int> next = d.Lambda;

The outer method also reads and writes d.count instead of a local, which is why both see the same variable. One helper object is made for each scope that holds captured variables, so a variable declared inside a loop gets a new object on each pass (which is why the copy trick works). This is also why closures allocate memory.

A static lambda (C# 9) is a lambda marked static that is not allowed to capture anything from the method around it.

int factor = 3;
Func<int, int> a = x => x * factor;           // captures factor, allocates a closure
Func<int, int> b = static x => x * 2;         // fine
Func<int, int> c = static x => x * factor;    // compile error: cannot capture

It gives you two things: no hidden closure object, so no allocation per call site, and a guarantee that you did not capture something by accident, such as this, which can keep a large object alive. Use it on hot paths and in callbacks that are stored for a long time. A static local function does the same.

A closure keeps every variable it captured alive for as long as the closure itself is reachable. If the closure lives for a long time, so does everything it points to.

class Page
{
    byte[] bigData = new byte[50_000_000];
    public void Hook() => AppEvents.Tick += () => Refresh();   // captures 'this'
}

A static event now holds a lambda that holds the Page, which holds the 50 MB array, so the page is never collected even after it is closed. Other cases: a closure put in a static cache, a timer, or a long-running task; and the compiler can share one helper object between lambdas, so a short lambda may keep alive variables that only a long one needs.

Fixes: unsubscribe, use a static lambda and pass what you need as arguments, or copy only the small value you need into a local first.

code.title: Lambda, anonymous method and local function compared

followUps:
Yes. A lambda has two forms: an expression body (x => x * 2) and a statement body with braces and a return.

Func<int, string> f = n =>
{
    if (n < 0) return "negative";
    var s = n.ToString();
    return "value " + s;
};

Use the expression form for one-line logic and the statement form when you need local variables, loops, if, try or several returns. An expression-bodied lambda for an Action can be any call, even one that returns a value, because the value is just dropped. Lambdas also support async (async x => await Save(x)), but not yield return.

A method group conversion is when you give a method's name where a delegate is expected, and the compiler builds the delegate from that method.

string[] words = { "1", "2", "3" };
words.Select(int.Parse);          // method group: same as x => int.Parse(x)
words.ToList().ForEach(Console.WriteLine);   // same as s => Console.WriteLine(s)

It is shorter and is read well when the method does exactly what the delegate needs. A caution: with overloaded methods the compiler picks the overload that matches the delegate type, which can surprise you. For example int.Parse has overloads that take a culture, and Select((s, i) => ...) with an index passes the index as a second argument. Before C# 11 each such conversion also created a new delegate on every call; newer compilers cache it.

It means the compiler can work out the delegate type of a lambda by itself, so you can store it in var instead of writing Func<...>.

var add = (int a, int b) => a + b;       // Func<int, int, int>
var log = (string s) => Console.WriteLine(s);   // Action<string>
var bad = x => x * 2;                    // error: parameter type unknown

It works when every parameter has a type written out (the return type is worked out from the body). Before C# 10 you needed Func<int, int, int> add = .... C# 10 also lets you add attributes and an explicit return type to a lambda, and C# 12 allows default values for lambda parameters. This is mostly handy in minimal APIs: app.MapGet("/", (int id) => ...).

code.title: Expression trees: a lambda as data, then compiled and run

followUps:
Because a Func is opaque compiled code, so EF Core cannot turn it into SQL. The only thing it can do is run the filter on every row in memory, so first it must download the whole table.

Func<Order, bool> f = o => o.Total > 100;
db.Orders.Where(f).ToList();        // IEnumerable.Where: SELECT * FROM Orders, then filter in C#

db.Orders.Where(o => o.Total > 100).ToList();   // Expression: SELECT ... WHERE Total > 100

The danger is that the code compiles in both cases. It happens when you pass a stored Func variable, or a method that takes Func instead of Expression<Func>, or you call a method like AsEnumerable() before Where. With a million rows that is a million rows over the network.

Build the expression tree yourself from a whitelist of allowed fields and operators, and pass user values as constants (which EF turns into SQL parameters). Never build query text from the input.

var p = Expression.Parameter(typeof(Product), "p");
var prop = Expression.Property(p, allowedField);           // only names from your list
var test = Expression.Equal(prop, Expression.Constant(value));
var filter = Expression.Lambda<Func<Product, bool>>(test, p);
db.Products.Where(filter);

Safety rules: map the user's field name to a property through a dictionary (unknown names are rejected), limit operators to a fixed set, convert the value to the property's type, and cap the number of conditions. Alternatives are a library such as System.Linq.Dynamic.Core with a strict whitelist, or a fixed set of optional filters: if (name != null) q = q.Where(...).

Because Compile() generates new IL code at run time and loads it, which takes from tens of microseconds to several milliseconds, much more than running the delegate. If you compile on every call, that cost repeats every time.

static readonly Func<Order, bool> IsBig = ((Expression<Func<Order, bool>>)(o => o.Total > 100)).Compile();
IsBig(order);    // compile once, call many times

Typical pattern: compile once in a static field, or in a ConcurrentDictionary keyed by the expression's shape. Generated code is also not collected quickly. In a loop of a million calls, the difference is seconds against a few milliseconds. Note that EF Core does not call Compile() for queries; it translates the tree and caches the result itself, and EF.CompileQuery exists for hot queries.

code.title: try, catch, finally: order of execution and the exception hierarchy

followUps:
Yes. The finally block runs after the return value has been worked out and before control actually leaves the method.

int F()
{
    try { return 1; }
    finally { Console.WriteLine("cleanup"); }   // prints, then F returns 1
}

It also runs after break, continue and goto, and when an exception is passing through. It does not run if the process is killed, the machine loses power, Environment.FailFast is called, or the thread is in an endless loop. Avoid putting a return inside finally (not allowed in C#). Changing a variable in finally after a return x does not change the value already being returned for value types.

The new exception replaces the one that was being handled, and the original is lost unless you keep it.

try { throw new Exception("first"); }
finally { throw new Exception("second"); }   // caller sees only "second"

The caller never learns about "first", so the real cause is hidden and debugging is hard. So keep finally simple and unable to fail: release resources, close handles and so on. If cleanup can fail, wrap it in its own try/catch inside finally and log the problem. Better still, use using or IDisposable, as the framework's Dispose methods are written not to throw. If you must report both, throw an AggregateException that contains both.

Because it means a bug in your code, and catching it hides the bug instead of fixing it. A null reference means you used something that was not set up; the right response is to prevent it, not to handle it afterwards.

  • The cause is usually a missing check or a wrong assumption, and the program is probably in a wrong state, so continuing is unsafe.
  • Catching it means swallowing the stack trace that tells you which line is wrong.
  • Throwing is expensive; a null check costs almost nothing.

Instead: validate at the edges (ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(x)), turn on nullable reference types, and use ?. and ??. The same holds for IndexOutOfRangeException and InvalidCastException. Let them reach the global handler, which logs them and returns a 500.

code.title: throw versus throw ex: what the stack trace shows

followUps:
An inner exception is the original error that caused the one you are looking at. You use it when you catch a low-level problem and throw a more meaningful one, without losing the cause.

try { repo.Save(order); }
catch (SqlException ex)
{
    throw new OrderFailedException($"Could not save order {order.Id}", ex);   // ex becomes InnerException
}

The caller sees a message in business terms, and the logs show the whole chain: ex.InnerException, then its own inner exception, and so on. ex.ToString() prints the full chain, and most logging frameworks do this for you. Always pass the original as the inner exception when you wrap, so the stack trace and database error number are not lost.

Use ExceptionDispatchInfo. Capture the exception while you are in the catch block, and call Throw() later; it rethrows the same exception with its original stack trace, and adds a marker line showing where it was rethrown.

ExceptionDispatchInfo edi = null;
try { Work(); }
catch (Exception ex) { edi = ExceptionDispatchInfo.Capture(ex); }

Cleanup();
edi?.Throw();     // original trace kept

This is what await does for you when a task fails, and it is used in code that collects errors from several threads. For a single error, edi.SourceException gives the object back. Use throw; instead whenever you are still inside the catch block.

Because the same error is logged several times, each time with less context, and the logs fill with noise that hides the real problem.

catch (Exception ex)
{
    _log.LogError(ex, "Repo failed");   // layer 1
    throw;
}
// layer 2 does the same, then layer 3 ...  one failure = 3 to 6 log entries

When an alert fires, an on-call person sees six errors and thinks there are six failures. Counts and dashboards are wrong too. The better rule: catch only where you can handle the error, or where you add useful information (wrap with an inner exception and context). Log once, at the boundary where the error is finally handled, such as the global exception middleware. In between, just let it travel up.

code.title: A custom exception with extra data, and a result object for expected failures

followUps:
Because Microsoft's own guidance says it is obsolete: it was meant as the base for exceptions thrown by applications, but the framework itself never followed that split, so it adds no meaning.

The recommendation is to derive custom exceptions straight from Exception (or from a fitting built-in one, such as InvalidOperationException, ArgumentException). A deep hierarchy only makes catch blocks harder to write, and nobody catches ApplicationException as a group. Name the class with the Exception suffix, make it public if callers must catch it, and give it the usual constructors (empty, message, message plus inner) if the type is used in a library. Add useful properties, like an id or amount.

Use a result object, because a taken email is a normal, expected outcome of the user's input, not an exceptional failure.

  • Cost: a throw takes microseconds up to milliseconds; a returned value takes nanoseconds. Under load, thousands of duplicate sign-ups can slow a server.
  • Clarity: the signature Result Register(...) tells the caller to check the outcome. An exception can be forgotten.
  • Noise: exceptions show up in logs and debuggers ("break on first-chance exceptions") as if something was broken.

Use exceptions for things that should not happen: lost database connection, a null argument, a corrupt file. A rule of thumb: if you can predict it and it happens during normal use, return a result (or a TryXxx method); if it is a surprise, throw.

Catch each custom exception type in one place, the global handler, and turn it into a status code and a standard error body.

ExceptionStatus
validation failed400 Bad Request (or 422)
not authenticated401
not allowed403
NotFoundException404
conflict, e.g. duplicate or stale version409
anything else500, with a generic message
var (status, title) = ex switch
{
    NotFoundException => (404, "Not found"),
    ConflictException => (409, "Conflict"),
    _ => (500, "Server error")
};

Use IExceptionHandler (ASP.NET Core 8 and later) and return ProblemDetails. Never put stack traces or database messages in the response body.

code.title: Exception best practices: guard clauses, finally cleanup and one place to log

followUps:
An exception filter is a when condition on a catch block: the block runs only if the condition is true, and otherwise the exception keeps travelling as if that catch did not exist.

catch (HttpRequestException ex) when (ex.StatusCode == HttpStatusCode.NotFound)
{
    return null;
}

It is better than catching and rethrowing because the stack is not unwound until a catch really accepts the exception, so the original stack and local variables stay intact for a debugger or a crash dump, and there is no extra rethrow cost. Filters are also a neat place to log without handling (when (Log(ex)) where Log returns false). Keep filter code simple: if it throws, the exception is dropped and the filter counts as false.

Treat it as a normal way for the work to end, not as an error: stop quickly, clean up, and do not log it as a failure.

Cancellation is signalled with OperationCanceledException (or TaskCanceledException) when the user closes the browser or a timeout fires.

try { await DoWorkAsync(ct); }
catch (OperationCanceledException) when (ct.IsCancellationRequested)
{
    _log.LogInformation("Cancelled");   // not LogError
    throw;                              // let the caller know
}

Pass the CancellationToken into every async call, do not catch it with a general catch (Exception) that swallows it, and do not return a 500 for it. ASP.NET Core ignores the exception when RequestAborted fired, because nobody is waiting for the response.

It hides every failure: the program carries on as if nothing happened, with wrong or missing data, and nobody ever finds out why.

try { SaveOrder(order); }
catch (Exception) { }          // the order is lost, the customer sees "success"

Problems: the real cause and stack trace disappear; it also catches things you must not stop, such as OutOfMemoryException, ThreadAbort-style failures and cancellation; and the state is probably broken, so later code fails in a confusing place. If you really can ignore an error (closing a socket that is already closed), catch the one specific type, add a comment explaining why, and log at debug level. Otherwise either handle it properly or let it go up to the global handler.

code.title: Global exception handling: a middleware pipeline built from delegates

followUps:
Because you would repeat the same try/catch, the same logging and the same response shape in every action, and one forgotten action returns a different error format or leaks details.

  • Duplication: hundreds of identical blocks that drift apart.
  • Inconsistent output: one action returns a stack trace, another a plain string.
  • Hidden code: the real logic is surrounded by error handling.
  • Double logging when the middleware also logs.

A controller should do its job and throw (or return a result) when something is wrong. One IExceptionHandler (or UseExceptionHandler) maps exception types to status codes. Local catch blocks are still fine when the action can recover or add information, such as turning a database duplicate-key error into a 409.

Exception middleware wraps the whole pipeline and sees every exception from any later step (routing, auth, endpoints, other middleware). An exception filter runs only around MVC controller actions and is part of the MVC pipeline.

Exception middleware / handlerMVC exception filter
Scopeentire app, including minimal APIscontrollers and Razor pages only
Access toHttpContextaction context, model state, action arguments
Sees errors fromeverything after itactions, action filters, result execution

In a modern API, use app.UseExceptionHandler() with an IExceptionHandler for the general case, and add a filter only when you need MVC-specific details.

Use ProblemDetails (RFC 9457) for every error, including the 400 validation response, so clients parse one shape.

  • With [ApiController], model-state errors already come back as a ValidationProblemDetails with an errors dictionary.
  • Call builder.Services.AddProblemDetails() so exception, 404 and 401 responses use the same shape.
  • For your own ValidationException, the handler builds Results.ValidationProblem(errors) or a ProblemDetails with the same errors extension.
{ "type": "...", "title": "One or more validation errors occurred.",
  "status": 400, "errors": { "Email": ["Email is required"] } }

Also add a trace id so support can find the log entry.

Make a deep copy by creating new objects for every nested reference, not just the top one. A normal assignment or MemberwiseClone() gives a shallow copy, so both copies would share the same inner objects.

  • Copy constructor or Clone() method: clear and fast, but you must write it and keep it up to date.
  • Records: with is shallow too, so nested lists are still shared.
  • Serialize and deserialize: JsonSerializer.Deserialize<T>(JsonSerializer.Serialize(obj)) copies a whole graph with little code, but it is slower and loses private state and cycles.

Test it: change a nested item in the copy and check that the original did not change. BinaryFormatter is removed; do not use it.

A cast (Dog)animal throws InvalidCastException when the object is not a Dog. The as operator returns null instead, and works only for reference and nullable types.

Dog d1 = (Dog)animal;     // exception if wrong
Dog d2 = animal as Dog;   // null if wrong
if (animal is Dog d3) { d3.Bark(); }   // test and cast in one step, best form

Use a cast when a wrong type is a bug. Use is with a pattern, or as plus a null check, when either type is possible. Also, a cast can call a user-defined conversion and convert numbers ((int)3.9), while as never converts, it only checks the type.

Make all state set once, in the constructor, with no way to change it afterwards, and make sure nested objects cannot change either.

public sealed class Order
{
    public string Id { get; }
    public IReadOnlyList<string> Lines { get; }
    public Order(string id, IEnumerable<string> lines)
    {
        Id = id;
        Lines = lines.ToList().AsReadOnly();   // own copy, so the caller's list is not shared
    }
    public Order WithLine(string line) => new Order(Id, Lines.Append(line));
}

The checklist: get-only or init properties, readonly fields, a private copy of any collection that is passed in, read-only types for what you expose, sealed (so a subclass cannot add mutable state), and "with"-style methods that return a new object. A record or record struct with init members does most of this in one line.

Because a static class cannot be used as an instance, and an interface contract is met by an instance: IFoo x = ... needs an object, and a static class cannot be created.

A static class has only static members, and it is sealed and abstract at the same time. Interfaces describe instance members that are called through an object, so the language gives no way to say "this static class is an IFoo".

What you can do: make a normal (singleton) class that implements the interface, so it can be injected and faked; or, from C# 11, declare static abstract members in an interface, which a type implements and generic code calls as T.Method(); even then, a static class cannot be the type argument.

Lazy<T> has three thread-safety modes, set by the LazyThreadSafetyMode value (or a bool in the constructor).

ModeBehaviour
ExecutionAndPublication (the default)a lock makes sure the factory runs once; other threads wait
PublicationOnlyseveral threads may run the factory, the first finished result wins and the others are thrown away; no lock held while it runs
Noneno locking, for single-threaded use; fastest

With the default mode, if the factory throws, the exception is cached and thrown again on every .Value call. In PublicationOnly mode it is not cached, so another attempt can succeed. Use the default unless you have measured a problem.

No. A struct cannot inherit from a class or from another struct. Every struct derives directly from System.ValueType, and structs are implicitly sealed.

A struct can still:

  • implement any number of interfaces;
  • override the virtual methods of object (ToString, Equals, GetHashCode);
  • contain other structs or class references as fields.

Why: a struct variable holds its fields in a fixed amount of memory, so a bigger derived struct would not fit, and there is no type header for virtual dispatch. If you need shared behaviour, share it with an interface (and default methods), a helper static class, or composition.

Return IEnumerable<T> when callers only need to loop over the results, because it promises less, so you can change the implementation later and may stream the items without building them all.

  • Flexibility: today a List, tomorrow a lazy yield method or a database stream, with no change for callers.
  • Safety: callers cannot call Add or Clear on your internal list (they could still cast it back, so return a copy or a read-only wrapper).
  • Memory: an iterator hands out one item at a time.

Return IReadOnlyList<T> or List<T> when callers need Count or index access, to avoid repeated enumeration. A lazy IEnumerable run twice does the work twice, and may hit a disposed database context.

yield return x gives the next item to the caller and pauses the method; yield break ends the sequence at once, with no more items.

IEnumerable<int> Take(IEnumerable<int> src, int n)
{
    if (n <= 0) yield break;        // empty sequence
    int i = 0;
    foreach (var x in src)
    {
        yield return x;            // give one item, then pause here
        if (++i == n) yield break; // stop early
    }
}

Reaching the end of the method also ends the sequence, so yield break is needed only for an early exit. You cannot use return value in an iterator, and you cannot put yield inside a try with a catch, or in a finally.

Not if the exception is never caught anywhere in the process. In that case the runtime may end the process without running the finally blocks.

An unhandled exception normally runs the unhandled-exception event and then the process is terminated; whether finally blocks lower in the stack run is not guaranteed in that case. The first pass of the exception system looks for a matching catch, and if none exists, the second pass that runs the finally blocks may never start. Console apps often seem to run them, but do not rely on it.

The consequence: never depend on finally alone for something critical such as releasing a distributed lock or committing a file. Give such data a timeout or an owner that can recover it, and add a global handler (AppDomain.UnhandledException, IHostApplicationLifetime) to log and shut down cleanly.
